storm.summary_layperson: Showers and storms are around the region but the nearby cells are tracking away from us, and the cool Sound is running an unusually strong buffer this afternoon — anything that does come across the water should reach the cove weaker than it looks inland.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Sound water at 75°F against 86°F air gives an 11°F gap that holds right through the afternoon and only fades around 8:52 PM, so the cove's protective layer is at full strength for the whole window.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture. Radar shows cells 19–40 miles out to the west-northwest, west and west-southwest, topping around 52 dBZ. The system is moving toward the west-northwest at about 37 kt — every tracked cell is currently opening the distance from the cove, not closing on it. There is no arrival time to give, because nothing is inbound.

There is still fuel around. Instability sits at 1,870 J/kg of CAPE (the energy available for thunderstorms) with 24 kt of deep-layer wind shear, and the NWS carries a slight chance of showers and storms through the afternoon. That combination is enough for a cell to fire more or less overhead rather than arrive from elsewhere. A Heat Advisory and an Air Quality Alert are both in effect.

The Sound is running a strong buffer today. Long Island Sound is 74.7°F against 86°F inland air — an 11.3°F gap. Because water holds its temperature while land heats up and then cools off, that gap is not a fixed number: it stays wide all afternoon, and only closes below the level that matters at about 8:52 PM, once the evening air has cooled toward the water temperature. For this 1–5 PM window the layer is at full strength the entire time.

What that means for the cove. A wide gap puts a stable layer of air over the water that starves the low levels of an approaching storm. Today's cells sit to the west and west-northwest, so anything that did turn back toward us would cross the Sound on the way in and run into that layer — the geometry that gives the cove its biggest advantage. Expect the cove to see wind without the rain and thunder that inland Fairfield and Westchester get from the same cell.

What would change the call. Two things. If instability climbs past about 3,000 J/kg, a storm can punch straight through the stable layer instead of being choked by it — worth watching, though today's 1,870 is comfortably short of that. And after roughly 8:52 PM the buffer is gone: a cell arriving late this evening should be taken at face value, with no discount for the Sound.

wind.regime_label: Sea breeze reinforced by the background southwesterly

hourly.shift_note: still full strength, no fade yet

wind.tactics_blurb: Classic SSW sea breeze at 9–11 kt with slight channeling along the west shore, so the right side pays on the first beat. Start toward the boat end, get out to the right early, then sail the oscillations back.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
The regime call. Both ingredients for a sea breeze are firmly in place: the land–water temperature difference is 11.3°F (inland air at 86°F against 74.7°F Sound water), well past the 5°F it needs, and the background weather-system wind is a modest 9 kt from the southwest. An onshore background wind like that does not fight the sea breeze — it reinforces it. This is the reliable summer pattern: stronger and steadier than a pure thermal day, and it will hold later into the evening because when the thermal fades the background flow remains.

Direction has been corrected upward. The model puts the breeze at S 187°, but stations across the western Sound are already at SSW 208° — the model systematically under-resolves the way a sea breeze rotates clockwise through the afternoon. A +15° maturation correction is applied, giving a corrected SSW around 197–203° for the window, and direction confidence is high. Riverside YC's own anemometer reads SSW 196° at 9.6 kt averaged over ten minutes, which backs that up on the water.

Why the right side. The cove runs north–south and opens due south into the Sound. A SSW breeze comes in cleanly off the water but channels slightly along the western shore past Belle Haven and Indian Harbor, which puts a little more pressure on the right-hand side of the beat looking upwind. It is a modest edge, not a huge one — worth getting out to early rather than defending all race.

Shift character. This is a mature sea breeze now rather than a filling one, so expect it to oscillate in a range of roughly ten degrees either side of 200° rather than trending persistently one way. Sail the shifts, and do not over-commit to a corner chasing pressure that will come back. Speed builds through the early afternoon and holds around 11 kt from 3 PM onward.

What the fleet will feel. Nine to eleven knots gusting 13 is a proper full-hiking breeze for dinghies and a good, honest keelboat day — enough to reward hiking and sail trim without being survival conditions. Sunset is at 8:04 PM, more than three hours after the window closes, so there is no thermal collapse to plan around; if you keep racing past 5 PM the breeze should stay with you well into the evening.

data_caveats: HRRR does not output a gust field — gusts estimated from Riverside YC's live gust-to-mean ratio (1.18×)
Model is running about 2 kt below Riverside YC's 10-minute average — hourly speeds anchored to the observed wind rather than raw model output
Direction includes the +15° sea-breeze maturation correction; the raw model reads 15–20° further left
Sea-breeze fractions at 50% of coastal stations with the mid-Sound buoy flipped but Long Island's north shore not — this is a Sound-driven sea breeze, not the full Atlantic one pushing across
Heat Advisory in effect through 8 PM tomorrow; Air Quality Alert also active
No storm arrival time given — all tracked cells are moving away from the cove
